candidates.attacker_control: Untrusted HTML passed to the default SAX entry points (AntiSamy.scan(String) -> AntiSamySAXScanner, AntiSamy.java:72-74/126-130, and AntiSamy.scan(Reader,Writer,Policy)). The attacker controls element names and all text/child content, including a `<s>` element (a normal HTML strikethrough element that the bundled antisamy-tinymce.xml allows with action="validate").
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checkstyle/format aside, the line has no comment justifying suffix matching; the sibling DOM implementation uses `"style".equals(tagNameLowerCase)` (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:395), strongly indicating equality was intended. `<style>` itself is still detected ("style".endsWith("style") is true), so the flaw only adds false positives. NekoHTML lowercases element names (names/elems=lower in AntiSamySAXScanner.getParser / AntiSamyDOMScanner.getDomParser), so case tricks are not needed. I checked that the CSS output is bounded by policy regexes that exclude `<`, `>`, and quotes, and that the transform output writer is the xerces HTML serializer, which escapes text; hence I do not claim demonstrated script injection. I also verified no other reversed equals/endsWith comparisons exist elsewhere in scope. No runtime confirmation was performed.
candidates.impact: Attacker-influenced content that should be validated/kept as HTML is instead routed through the CSS parser: policy-permitted child markup is silently destroyed, plain text is re-emitted only if it happens to parse as CSS, and CSS-parser output is written back into the HTML document inside the wrongly classified element. This is a sanitizer logic/state confusion (different behavior between the two supported scanners, content integrity loss, and content re-emission through an unintended parser). Direct script execution was not established from source: the HTML serializer escapes `<`/`>` in text nodes and the shipped CSS value regexes exclude angle brackets, so this is reported as a lead, not a proven XSS.
candidates.prerequisites: Use of the SAX scan path and a policy that gives action="validate" to an element whose name is a suffix of "style" (the shipped antisamy-tinymce.xml does this for `<s>`, antisamy-tinymce.xml:127; custom policies could enable st/sty/e/l/y/t). The affected element must pass tag/attribute validation so the ACTION_VALIDATE branch is reached.
candidates.root_cause: MagicSAXFilter.startElement computes `boolean isStyle = "style".endsWith(element.getLocalpart());` (src/main/java/org/owasp/validator/html/scan/MagicSAXFilter.java:302). The receiver and argument are reversed, so the check is true for every element name that is a suffix of the literal "style" (s, st, sty, styl, tyle, le, e, y, l, t) instead of only the element named "style". The equivalent DOM code uses the intended equality test (`"style".equals(tagNameLowerCase)`, AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:395), confirming the intended semantics.
candidates.title: SAX scanner treats tags whose names are suffixes of "style" (e.g. <s>) as CSS containers due to reversed endsWith comparison
candidates.trace: 1) AntiSamy.scan(taintedHtml) selects AntiSamySAXScanner (default = SAX). 2) MagicSAXFilter.startElement receives `<s>`; policy lookup returns a validate Tag; `isStyle` is wrongly true (302). 3) After attribute validation the code pushes Ops.CSS and starts recording `cssContent` (404-407). 4) characters() appends raw text of the subtree to cssContent (111); nested startElement calls under Ops.CSS push Ops.REMOVE, so all child elements and their attributes are discarded without HTML-policy processing (281-284). 5) endElement sees Ops.CSS, pops it and runs CssScanner.scanStyleSheet on the accumulated text (175-205), then re-emits the element plus the cleaned CSS text of the CSS parser (`super.startElement(element, cssAttributes, augs)`, characters(cleanHtml), endElement). 6) Consequently the DOM scanner and SAX scanner produce different sanitization for the same input/policy.
candidates.unverified: Whether the upstream project intended `equals` here (no VCS history or patched copy is available in scope), whether a serializer path ever emits the CSS-derived text unescaped, and whether any concrete payload yields script execution rather than content loss. The full exploitation depends on the deployed policy and on how the cleaned output is re-parsed by the consuming browser.
candidates.weakness_type: Incorrect comparison leading to improper sanitization (CWE-697/CWE-436, XSS-class sanitizer state confusion)

coverage_summary: Reviewed all 58 in-scope files reported by get_source_scope: 25 Java sources under src/main/java (scanner classes AntiSamy.java, AntiSamyDOMScanner, AntiSamySAXScanner, MagicSAXFilter, AbstractAntiSamyScanner, ASHTMLSerializer, Constants; CSS classes CssScanner, CssValidator, CssHandler, CssParser; policy/model classes Policy, InternalPolicy, Attribute, Tag, Property, AntiSamyPattern, TagMatcher, CleanResults, exceptions; util classes URIUtils, XMLUtil, HTMLEntityEncoder, ErrorMessageUtil), the five shipped policy XMLs and locale bundles, pom.xml, README/SECURITY, and CI configs. Traced the HTML input path end-to-end for both DOM and SAX scanners, including attribute/URL/CSS validation, comment/CDATA handling, style handling, and serialization. Security-relevant regexes (onsiteURL/offsiteURL/cssOnsiteUri/cssOffsiteUri/selector rules) were compared across the five policies for consistency. No tests are present in the snapshot; nothing was executed.
limitations: No test sources, upstream git history, patch, or patched/other-version artifact is available in scope, so the intended behavior of the flagged line and any later fix could not be diffed; conclusions are inferred from internal consistency (DOM vs SAX implementations).
No dependency jars/binaries are available, so xerces HTMLSerializer/NekoHTML behavior (text escaping, CDATA emission, tag balancing) was reasoned about, not verified at runtime.
The antisamy.xsd referenced by Policy is absent from the snapshot, so full policy schema conformance and include-handling behavior could not be exercised.
The ~2,700-line antisamy.xml and the other policy files were spot-checked on security-critical regexes/attributes rather than exhaustively diffed line-by-line against upstream.
No build, test, scanner, or exploit execution was performed (prohibited); all findings are source-level leads, not runtime-confirmed vulnerabilities.

rejected_leads.lead: MagicSAXFilter validates the `style` attribute before/without checking whether the policy allows a style attribute for that tag (`if ("style".equalsIgnoreCase(name))` at MagicSAXFilter.java:322 runs regardless of `attribute == null`), while AntiSamyDOMScanner.processAttributes requires `attr != null` (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:577). A style attribute can therefore survive on tags whose policy omits it.
rejected_leads.reason: Inconsistency is real, but with all bundled policies style is either a global attribute or the CSS rules are empty, so the surviving value is CSS-scanned/empty; no security impact could be established from source alone. Kept as an unconfirmed, lower-ranked lead.

rejected_leads.lead: Policy.getDocumentElementByUrl/resolveEntity validate only the base URL (`verifyLocalUrl(baseUrl)`) and then resolve `<include href=...>`/system IDs with `new URL(baseUrl, href)` and `openStream()`, so a policy file containing a remote include could cause an outbound fetch despite the javadoc promising local-only URLs.
rejected_leads.reason: Requires control of the policy file, which is trusted configuration rather than the untrusted HTML input this sanitizer is designed to handle; also documented as a local-URL-only API. Hardening/trust-boundary issue, not the strongest candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: AntiSamyDOMScanner.stripNonValidXMLCharacters uses `invalidXmlCharsMatcher.matches()` (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:824), so invalid XML characters (NUL/control characters) are only removed when the entire input consists of them; normal-looking input keeps them and relies on NekoHTML.
rejected_leads.reason: Long-standing upstream quirk; no parser-differential or XSS consequence could be demonstrated from the available source.

rejected_leads.lead: SAX path passes CDATA character data through to the serializer and only records an error (MagicSAXFilter.java:114-118), unlike the DOM scanner which converts CDATA to a text node (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:730-737).
rejected_leads.reason: The xerces HTML serializer normally escapes text; whether any configuration emits the CDATA content raw could not be verified without the serializer sources/jars. Unconfirmed.

rejected_leads.lead: XMLUtil.decode/encode use Matcher.matches() rather than find(), decoding only when the whole string is a single entity.
rejected_leads.reason: Affects policy-file parsing of trusted configuration values, not attacker HTML; no security impact established.

summary: AntiSamy 1.7.6-SNAPSHOT HTML/CSS sanitizer review. I read all 58 in-scope files (scanner, CSS, policy, model, util classes, five policy XMLs, properties, build/CI files) and traced the SAX and DOM sanitization paths. The single strongest source-supported lead is in the SAX scanner: MagicSAXFilter computes the \"is this element a style container?\" test with a reversed endsWith (`"style".endsWith(element.getLocalpart())`), so any validated element whose name is a suffix of \"style\" (notably `<s>`, allowed by the bundled antisamy-tinymce.xml) is switched into CSS mode instead of being processed as HTML. The DOM scanner uses the correct equality test, confirming the intended check. Impact is a sanitizer state/comparison confusion (wrong parser applied to attacker-controlled content; child markup silently dropped, textual content re-parsed and re-emitted as CSS). I could not demonstrate direct script execution because the serializer escapes text and shipped CSS regexes disallow angle brackets, so I report it as a lead rather than a confirmed exploit. Rejected leads and limitations are listed.
